@graph.headline: Crypto Crisis Communications in 2026: Exploits, Hacks and Depegs
@graph.alternativeHeadline: A field guide to running comms through an exploit, hack or depeg, with holding-statement template and trust-rebuild sequence
@graph.description: When a crypto exploit or depeg hits, the first sixty minutes decide the narrative. This 2026 crisis comms playbook covers the holding-statement template, hour-by-hour response timeline, do-and-don't list, media briefing strategy, and the four-step trust-rebuild sequence most protocols skip.

itemListElement.name: Crypto Crisis Communications in 2026: Exploits, Hacks and Depegs

mainEntity.name: What should a crypto protocol post in the first hour of a hack?

acceptedAnswer.text: A holding statement, published within sixty minutes of internal confirmation. It should confirm you are aware of the incident, tell users the one thing they need to do right now (pause deposits, bridge out, take no action), and give a specific time by which you will provide a fuller update. It does not need root cause, attribution or compensation details. Speed and clarity matter more than completeness at this stage. Post it on your official Twitter/X and Discord simultaneously.

mainEntity.name: How is crisis comms for a depeg different from an exploit?

acceptedAnswer.text: A depeg is not a security incident, so the messaging frame is different. You cannot frame it as an attack. The communication needs to explain market mechanics honestly, give users specific actions to protect their positions, and lay out the protocol's path back to stability with realistic timelines. Teams that run an exploit playbook on a depeg, emphasising investigation and attacker speculation, confuse users and compound the credibility damage.

mainEntity.name: Should you brief journalists before publishing a public statement?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The public statement comes first, always, so your community hears from you directly rather than reading a reporter's reconstruction. After the holding statement is live, brief three to five beat reporters personally, offer a direct technical briefing, and provide your named spokesperson. The goal is accurate coverage, not favourable coverage. Reporters who can reach you in a crisis write better stories than those who cannot.

mainEntity.name: What does trust rebuilding after an exploit actually look like?

acceptedAnswer.text: Four things in sequence: a re-audit engagement announcement naming the auditor, full publication of the audit results including any findings, a founder-led account of what the team learned (op-ed or long-form interview), and then the relaunch narrative. Skipping to the relaunch without the preceding three steps leaves the incident as the dominant narrative at exactly the moment you need a fresh start. The sequence matters as much as the individual pieces.

mainEntity.name: How much does crisis PR cost in crypto?

acceptedAnswer.text: A retained fractional PR operator who covers crisis preparedness runs $5,000 to $12,000 per month, and that relationship is in place before anything happens. A reactive crisis retainer, engaged after an incident is already in motion, costs significantly more and starts from zero context. A full agency runs $15,000 to $45,000 per month. The preparation gap is the most expensive thing most protocols overlook in their comms budget.
